### I. The Edge of the Shelf

The station sits upon a spit of dark slate three miles south of a town that has spent two centuries forgetting itself. To reach it, one must walk the shingle at low water, picking a path between the bladderwrack and the ribs of drowned skiffs, or wait for the tractor that comes on Tuesdays, its iron wheels caked with wet sand and dead kelp. Most choose neither; most stay behind the sea wall, where the chimneys smoke turf and the harbor cats sleep beneath overturned dories.

The tide-house itself is octagonal, built in 1884 from dressed granite blocks hauled by barge from the quarries at Penmaenmawr. It was designed to withstand the fetch of the whole North Atlantic—a long, brutal stretch of gray water that builds its momentum somewhere off the coast of Greenland, gathers weight across three thousand miles of empty shelf, and breaks against this headland with the concussive thump of a dropped engine block.

Inside, at the center of the flagstone floor, is the well: an iron pipe eighteen inches in diameter that descends through twenty feet of living rock into the sea beneath. Within that pipe floats a hollow copper cylinder the size of a loaf of bread. As the tide rises, the float rises; as the tide ebbs, it sinks. A counterweighted bronze cable runs from the float up through the floorboards to the recording apparatus on my desk—a machine known to the Admiralty as a Thompson Tide Gauge, though it looks less like a gauge than like a clock that has lost its mind to music.

It has a brass cylinder twenty-four inches long, driven by a clockwork escapement that ticks with the dry, deliberate cadence of a beetle in dry timber. Wrapped around this drum is a sheet of coordinate paper, ruled in pale violet ink into twenty-four hours across its circumference and twenty feet along its length. A sapphire-tipped stylus, linked to the bronze cable by a reduction gear of microscopic accuracy, rests against the paper. As the sea breathes through the rock, the cylinder turns and the stylus rises and falls, drawing an endless, looping sinusoid—a cardiogram of the ocean’s ribs.

I have tended this machine for fourteen years.

Before me, my uncle tended it for thirty-two. When his knees swelled to the size of turnips and he could no longer make the crossing over the shingle, he sat in his Windsor chair by the grate in the village, looking down at his slippers, and told me that the sea had no memory, which was why men had to keep one for it. He was wrong, of course. The sea is nothing *but* memory; it is only that its memory is recorded in a script we are generally too hurried or too terrified to read: in the redistribution of gravel, the migration of sandspits, the gradual tilting of drowned forests, and the salt that enters the pores of the stone and waits fifty winters to split it from the inside out.

My work consists of winding the twin springs every Saturday at midnight, replacing the blue ink in the sapphire reservoir with an eyedropper, changing the paper rolls on the first of each month, and keeping the ledger. The ledger is bound in green buckram, four inches thick, stamped in gold leaf that has faded to the color of wet straw: *STATION 44 – HYDROMETRY & LITTORAL DRIFT*.

Outside, the gulls sit along the parapet with their heads tucked into their breast feathers, all facing the wind like weathered vane-cocks. When the wind backs into the northeast, they turn together without a sound, a silent militia pivoting on greasy stone.

***

### II. On the Cartography of Phantoms

In 1875, the Hydrographic Office of the British Admiralty published a chart designated simply *No. 2060: North Atlantic Ocean*. It was, by all technical metrics, a masterwork of Victorian empiricism. The soundings were sparse in the mid-basin—lead lines lowered four miles through black water take half a day to heave back to the cathead—but the coasts were ruled with razor precision.

Yet scattered across that gray expanse were dozens of small, irregular shapes marked with the letters *E.D.* (*Existence Doubtful*) or *P.D.* (*Position Doubtful*). There was the Isle of Buss, reported by the survivors of Martin Frobisher’s third expedition in 1578; there was Verde Island, which had appeared on Spanish rutters since the conquest; there was the Saxemberg Island, sketched with lovely topography by a Dutch captain in 1670, complete with two distinct peaks and a column of white smoke rising from a wooded valley.

They did not exist. Or, rather, they existed only in that specific stratum of reality produced by fatigue, optical refraction, and the human brain’s frantic refusal to look at an empty horizon and accept its emptiness. A patch of low cumulus catching the sunset at forty miles can mimic a headland of red granite with such fidelity that the lookout will swear he sees sheep grazing upon the downland. An upwelling of cold water will flatten the chop into the appearance of a shoal; a dead whale, belly-up and bloated with gas, has been entered into the logs of three separate schooners as "a black reef, unapproachable by reason of surf."

We laugh at this now, equipped as we are with synthetic aperture radar and the cold, unblinking eyes of geostationary satellites that photograph the planet’s skin every twelve minutes down to the resolution of an abandoned garden rake. But we have merely traded maritime phantoms for digital ones.

Consider Sandy Island. It sat in the Coral Sea between New Caledonia and Australia, precisely at 19°13′S 159°56′E. It was mapped by the whaling ship *Velocity* in 1876; it was incorporated into British admiralty charts in 1908; it migrated into the databases of the world’s maritime agencies; it was digitized, verified by algorithmic cross-reference, and rendered into Google Earth as a long, dark finger of land six miles long, floating upon the blue pixels of the deep sea.

In November 2012, an Australian research vessel, the *Southern Surveyor*, sailed directly through the center of Sandy Island. The echo-sounders beneath the keel showed forty-six hundred feet of clear water. The island had lived for one hundred and thirty-six years not because anyone had seen it twice, but because no one had possessed the administrative nerve to erase it. It was an institutional ghost, preserved by the simple, terrible weight of documentation.

I keep a list of these vanished places pinned to the wainscoting above my washstand:

*   *Dougherty’s Island* (South Pacific; seen 1841, erased 1932)
*   *The Aurora Islands* (South Atlantic; three distinct peaks of black basalt, surveyed by the corvette *Atrevida* in 1794; gone by 1840)
*   *St. Matthew’s Shoal* (Atlantic equatorial; logged by the Portuguese in 1516; vanished after eighty years of navigational terror)
*   *Nimrod Islands* (sub-Antarctic; reported by Captain Wright in 1828; searched for by Shackleton; nothing found but gray petrels and floating drift-ice)

There is something immensely comforting in their erasure. It suggests that the surface of the earth still retains a small, recalcitrant capacity to disown us. We lay our grids down like iron fences, we name every knuckle of stone, we assign three words from a dictionary to every square yard of the Sahara Desert so that an ambulance can find a dying man who has fallen from a camel, but the planet still flexes its shoulders now and then and shrugs an entire archipelago into the abyss.

Once, during a gale in my third winter here, when the salt spray was hitting the northern glass so hard it sounded like handfuls of dried peas thrown against the pane, I saw an island four miles out. It was long, pale, and notched at its western end like the sight of a rifle. It stayed there from two in the afternoon until the dusk took it. I did not log it. To log it would have been to give it an entry into the great legal machinery of disappearance; it would have required my successors to watch for it, to doubt their eyes, to write letters to Taunton asking for a hydrographic cutter to verify its absence.

I let it stay where it was: an optical sediment, a trick of the spray and the failing light, an island made entirely of cold air and my own wish to see something out there besides water that did not care whether I lived or died.

***

### III. The Acoustics of the Grave Shift

Between the hours of two and five in the morning, the universe is governed by an entirely different set of physical laws.

The town across the bay does not truly sleep; it sinks. The electric streetlamps, which buzz during the early evening with a high, neurotic 60-cycle hum, seem to quiet their filament chatter. The few trawlers moored to the town quay pull against their spring lines with a slow, wet groan that travels across the low water like sound through an iron pipe.

In the tide-house, the silence is not an absence of sound, but an accumulation of tiny, mechanical frictions. The escapement wheel ticks: *click-rest, click-rest*. The bronze cable shifts a hair’s-breadth across its grooved pulley as the Atlantic swells two inches beneath the floorboards: *hiss*. The sapphire stylus makes a microscopic scratching noise as it drags its burden of blue ink across the heavy paper: *scritch*.

In the fourteenth century, before the democratization of the mechanical clock, Europeans practiced what historians now call the *biphasic sleep*. They would retire at dusk, sleep for four hours, and then wake naturally around midnight into a period called *the watch* or *the dorveille*.

For two hours, people did not fight their wakefulness. They did not roll over and check the glowing face of a telephone to see how many minutes of rest remained before their labor was demanded of them again. They rose. They stoked the embers of the hearth. They visited neighbors to borrow a cup of lard; they recited prayers that had no petition in them, only contemplation; they made love without haste, in the warmth of coarse wool blankets, while the frost grew its ferns across the inside of the unglazed windows.

It was during this interval that the brain operated in a state that has since been almost entirely eradicated from the western hemisphere: an unanxious, non-productive lucidity. It was the hour of poets, of thieves, and of women who knew the properties of dried vervain.

Out here, the dorveille is not an interval; it is a permanent climate.

When you sit alone in a room surrounded on seven sides by salt water (for the well brings the sea into the very belly of the building, and the spray covers the roof), the mind eventually sheds its domestic posture. It stops preparing for the next interaction. It stops rehearsing arguments that will never occur. It begins to resemble the room it occupies: austere, slightly damp, illuminated by a single unshaded sixty-watt bulb that hangs from a braided cord of brown silk, smelling of paraffin, salt, and brass polish.

I have spent many hours examining my fingers under this bulb. They are the fingers of a clerk, slightly flattened at the tips from forty years of turning heavy pages, the nails scored with the fine longitudinal ridges that doctors call *onychorrhexis*—the small, harmless corrugated tracks that age leaves behind, like the tracks of birds across mud before it turns to shale.

We are so frightened of these hours. We invent entire industries of sleep hygiene, of blue-light filters, of white-noise generators that simulate the sound of an Amazonian downpour for someone living in a studio apartment in Croydon who has never seen a tree larger than a municipal plane. We treat wakefulness at three in the morning as a pathology, an insurrection of the nerves, a failure of the will.

We cannot bear the thought of what is actually happening during those hours: which is that the world is carrying on perfectly well without our observation. The trees are exchanging nitrogen through their mycorrhizal networks in the woods behind the headland; the deep trenches are being swept by slow, abyssal currents that began their journey when the Romans were mining lead in the Mendips; the stars are burning through their hydrogen budgets with the cold, mathematical indifference of a banker closing an overdraft.

To be awake and idle at three in the morning is to be an unauthorized spectator at the rehearsal of our own absence.

***

### IV. The Silt Economy

The town of Dunwich, on the Suffolk coast, was once a great port. In the eleventh century, it had eight churches, three monasteries, a mint, and seventy-eight ships of the line. It had a harbor protected by a spit of shingle that had been laid down by the longshore drift over two thousand years.

In 1286, a northern storm cut the spit in half. In 1328, another gale swept through the breach, choked the mouth of the River Blyth with three hundred thousand tons of shingle in six hours, and turned the harbor into a stagnant lagoon. The town did not die immediately; it died parish by parish, street by street, butcher’s shop by butcher’s shop.

The cliffs at Dunwich are composed of what geologists call the Norwich Crag—a fragile, poorly consolidated layer of sand, silt, and ancient shells that has the structural integrity of brown sugar. When the sea hits the base of the crag, the cliff does not collapse with a dramatic crash; it simply slumps. It dissolves. The water turns the color of weak tea, and the next tide carries the sand south toward Orford Ness.

One by one, the churches went over the edge. St. Felix went first, around 1540. Then St. Leonard’s. Then St. John’s. In the winter of 1904, the last standing church, All Saints, had only its tower remaining on the edge of the drop. Visitors would travel from London on the Great Eastern Railway to see it: an ancient flint tower perched on the very brink of nothing, with the bones of the dead protruding from the exposed earth beneath it like roots.

An old postcard from that year shows a human femur sticking out of the cliff twelve feet below the turf line, pointing out across the sea like a bowsprit.

In 1919, the tower went down. A local fisherman reported that for three days after the collapse, when the water was flat calm after the November gales, you could hear the bells ringing beneath his keel as the swell rolled the flint boulders back and forth across the rubble of the nave.

This is the silt economy. Every coast is a transaction.

Here at Station 44, the transaction is currently in our favor, though it will not remain so. The spit is accreting. Every tide brings seventy tons of quartz gravel from the headland to the north and drops it along the eastern flank of our causeway. The spit is fattening, crawling slowly southward like an amoeba across the sea bed. In two hundred years, if the charts are correct, this octagonal tower will not be in the water at all; it will be marooned half a mile inland, surrounded by sea-buckthorn and sheep pastures, its iron well choked with dry sand, its bronze cable frozen in its grease.

The villagers think this is good news. They believe that land gained is a victory, that the earth is reclaiming what the sea had stolen.

They do not understand that the sea never loses. It merely lends. It is a creditor that works on a schedule so prolonged that the borrowers mistake the delay for an acquittal. Every grain of sand that gathers around my granite foundation has been torn from the living room of someone else’s house three miles up the coast. The spit is built of dead gardens, collapsed sheep-folds, and the gravel paths where young women in long skirts once walked out on Sunday afternoons to look at the water that would eventually swallow their parlors.

***

### V. The Philosophy of the Diaphone

A mile and a half out from my spit, anchored in forty fathoms of black water, is the *Gull Rock Light-Vessel*.

She is painted the color of dried ox-blood, with her name spelled out along her sides in letters six feet high: *G U L L*. She does not move; she has no engine, only two thirty-hundredweight mushroom anchors hooked into the mud beneath her, and a crew of four men who spend thirty days at a stretch staring at the salt on the galley skylight and listening to the radio from Cardiff.

Her main voice is not her lantern—lanterns are useless when the sea fog comes rolling off the Irish Sea like a wall of sheep’s wool—but her diaphone foghorn.

The diaphone is an instrument of terrifying beauty. It was invented in Canada by a man named John Northey, who had originally intended it to be an air pump for clearing mineshafts. It consists of a slotted piston that reciprocates inside a slotted cylinder, driven by compressed air at forty pounds per square inch. When the slots align, the air escapes in bursts of catastrophic violence: twenty thousand cubic feet of air per minute, expelled through a horn made of cast bronze twelve feet long.

Its note is an F-sharp two octaves below middle C.

It does not sound like a machine; it sounds like the planet itself groaning under the weight of its own rotation. When the *Gull* sounds her horn, the air inside my tide-house does not merely conduct the noise; it thickens with it. The water in the copper well trembles. The mercury in the barometer jumps a hundredth of an inch. If you are standing with your forehead against the granite wall, your teeth will vibrate in your jaw.

The note ends with what acousticians call the "grunt"—a sudden, sharp drop in frequency, down into the thirty-cycle range, caused by the deceleration of the piston as the air is cut off: *BWOOOOOO-OH*.

The purpose of that grunt is acoustic survival. High-frequency sounds are scattered by fog droplets; they lose themselves in the mist like sheep in a briar patch. But that low, guttural drop at the end of the blast can slip between the water particles. It hugs the surface of the sea, sliding through the cold, dense air immediately above the swell, traveling twenty miles through weather so thick that a captain cannot see his own jackstaff from the bridge wing.

Yet there is a thing known to seamen as the *acoustic shadow*.

It is one of the most terrifying phenomena in navigation. A vessel can be two miles from a diaphone horn, running through a white-out of sleet and fog, and hear nothing. Absolute silence. The lookouts strain their ears until their temples throb; the skipper checks his dead reckoning; the leadsman calls out thirty fathoms, twenty-five, twenty. Still nothing. The horn is blowing with all the force of three steam boilers behind it, but because of a thermal inversion—a layer of warm air sitting like a blanket over a layer of cold air—the sound waves are refracted upward. They curve over the ship like a vaulted ceiling, leaping clear over her masts, and plunge back down to hit the water four miles farther on.

The ship strikes the reef in total quiet, while a cottage four miles away has its tea-saucers rattling on the dresser.

I think of the acoustic shadow often when I read the letters my sister sends me from Leeds. She writes of her children, of the price of beef, of the new municipal bypass that has taken half her garden, of the small, dull indignities of an office that uses machines to calculate what three clerks used to do with ink and nibs. Her life seems to be lived entirely within the acoustic shadow of something monstrous. She can hear the teacups rattling, but she cannot hear the horn that is shaking them.

She writes: *“The town is very noisy now, Ronald. Even on Sundays, you can hear the lorries on the ring-road. Sometimes I think I would like to come out to your station for a month and just have the quiet.”*

I have never invited her. She thinks the quiet out here is an absence of noise. She does not know that the quiet out here is an iron bell that has been struck so hard, and so long ago, that the human ear can no longer hear the tone—it can only feel the displacement of the air against the skin.

***

### VI. The Sediment of the Margin

What does one find along the high-water mark after the equinoctial gales?

I have kept an inventory in the back of the ledger for thirty years, set down under the heading *FLOTSAM, JETSAM, & DERELICT*:

1.  *12th October 1898:* One crate of pickled herrings, marked *Stettin*, unbroken.
2.  *4th February 1902:* The figurehead of a schooner, representation of a woman with her hair bound in ribbons, painted blue; eyes missing, turned out by gulls or surf.
3.  *19th November 1911:* Three hundred and fourteen wooden spools for cotton thread, empty, unmarked.
4.  *2nd January 1916:* A life-belt from the steamship *Persia*, sunk off Crete three weeks prior. (How it came three thousand miles in twenty-two days against the prevailing drift is a matter I have referred to the Hydrographer; he has not replied.)
5.  *14th August 1923:* The skull of a pilot whale, half-cleaned by sea-lice, filled with fine gravel that smelled of engine grease.
6.  *27th March 1931:* A crate of green glass bottles containing water that was fresh, though stale; no label, no corks, sealed with red rosin.

And then there are the boots.

Every beach in the world that fronts the open sea is a graveyard for left boots. I do not know why they are almost invariably the left; my uncle had a theory that sailors, when abandoning a foundering vessel, always kicked off their right boot first in order to get a better purchase with their lead foot on the gunwale, but this is nonsense. The sea is simply asymmetrical. Its currents have a handedness, just as the molecules of sugar and tartaric acid have a handedness. The Coriolis effect turns the water to the right in the northern hemisphere; perhaps it turns the left boots to the land and carries the right ones to the Azores.

They are always of heavy cowhide, nailed with square iron brads that have rusted into little nodules of red oxide like rowan berries. The leather of the uppers does not rot quickly in salt water; it becomes slick, black, and supple as grease. It takes fifty years for the ocean to digest a good pair of sea-boots.

Sometimes, walking the shingle at sunrise, when the light is coming flat across the water from the direction of the Dutch sands, I will see one of them sitting upright among the bladderwrack, looking so purposeful, so attentively planted upon the gravel, that I have to stop and wait for the man who was wearing it to take his next step.

He never does. He is twenty miles out, down in the deep holes where the cod lie, his bones turned into ivory buttons by the hagfish and his blue wool frock worn away into silt by the dragging of the bottom-nets.

***

### VII. The Night of the Great Glass

The fourteenth of January, 1928, was the only time I have ever seen the Thompson Gauge run off the paper.

The morning had begun with a greasy yellow sky, the clouds low and flat, moving from the southeast with a greasy speed that left no wake behind them. The barometer at eight o'clock stood at 29.8 inches. By noon it had dropped to 29.1. By four in the afternoon, it was at 28.3—a fall so rapid that the pointer had moved like the minute hand of a kitchen clock.

When air pressure drops that quickly, the atmosphere stops being a weight that holds things down and becomes a vacuum that sucks them upward. The surface of the sea rose four feet before the wind even reached us; it was sucked up into the low-pressure core of the cyclone like water into a syringe.

The wind hit at five. It did not come as a gust; it came as a solid wall of air that smelled of rotten sponges and cold iron.

By eight, the causeway was four feet under. By ten, the waves were hitting the eastern face of the tide-house with such violence that the water was coming through the mortised seams of the granite blocks—not as a drip, but as a fine, vaporous fog that hung in the air like the spray from an atomizer. The single light bulb swung in a six-inch arc, its braided cord creaking against the brass hook in the ceiling.

I did not leave the room. There was nowhere to go; the spit was completely submerged, and the granite tower was an isolated pillar standing in five fathoms of foam.

At midnight, the float in the iron well came up to the stops. The bronze cable went slack for half a second as a monster swell lifted the tower’s skirt, then snapped tight with a twang like a bass fiddle. The sapphire stylus, which had never climbed higher than the eighteen-foot mark on the ruled sheet, reached the very top edge of the violet grid, slipped off the paper entirely, and began scratching its track directly into the polished brass of the cylinder.

I stood by the desk, holding the edge of the mahogany table with both hands to keep my footing as the floor thudded beneath my boots. Every time a wave took the northern bastion, the iron pipe in the floor acted like a piston in an engine: a column of green water and gray air was driven up through the well-head, spraying against the underside of the oak desk with a wet, flat *slap*.

It went on for nine hours.

The terrible thing about such storms is not their fury; it is their monotony. After the first three hours, the human capacity for terror is exhausted. The nervous system simply runs out of fuel. The noise—the roaring of the wind through the lantern ventilators, the crash of the water against the three-foot stone, the whine of the bronze cable, the dry ticking of the clockwork drum that carried on despite everything—became an architecture. It was no longer an event; it was the world.

I sat in my Windsor chair, wrapped in my oilskins, and ate two cold potatoes with salt from a chipped saucer.

Around three in the morning, during the absolute height of the gale, I felt something move beneath the floorboards that was not the shock of the water. It was a long, slow shudder that ran through the granite from the bedrock up: a lateral displacement that lasted no more than a second.

The spit had shifted.

Somewhere sixty feet below my chair, the slate strata had sheared along an ancient fault line—a seam of calcite that had held since the Devonian period, giving up its grip under the hydraulic pressure of ten thousand tons of water forced into its crevices at fifty miles an hour.

The tower leaned.

It leaned no more than a fraction of an inch—less than the thickness of a half-crown—but when you have watched a bronze plumb-bob hang over an iron floor for fourteen years, a fraction of an inch is as loud as a trumpet. The bob had moved out of the center of its brass ring; it sat there, shivering slightly, an eighth of an inch to the north-northeast.

The stylus, still scratching its blind mark into the bare brass of the cylinder, made a sudden, sharp dog-leg: a tiny, permanent scar across the metal that no emery cloth could ever take out.

And then, as suddenly as it had come, the core passed.

By six in the morning, the wind had veered into the northwest and dropped to a moderate gale. The sky through the eastern window turned from the color of wet lead to that strange, pale, watery lemon that belongs only to the mornings after shipwrecks.

I went out onto the gallery. The causeway had disappeared. Not washed away—covered. Three thousand tons of gray flint shingle had been piled across it by the tide, forming a new bank ten feet high, topped with yellow foam that the wind was blowing away in clotted lumps the size of sheep.

The town was still there across the bay, but it looked different. The church steeple had lost its lead flashing; the roof of the fish-house had been peeled back like the tin lid of a sardine tin; two schooners were high and dry in the salt marsh, lying on their sides with their topmasts tangled together like the legs of dead spiders.

I went back inside. I took my eyedropper, filled it with blue ink, and lowered the stylus back down onto the paper.

The sea was falling. The float was sinking through its pipe. The bronze cable was paying out through the reduction gears. The sapphire point found the coordinate line for seven in the morning, twelve feet above the low-water datum, and began once more to draw its smooth, perfect, indifferent curve across the grid.

***

### VIII. The Ledger of the End

My predecessor, my uncle, kept his ledgers with a steel crowquill nib that made a thin, querulous mark, like the scratches of a mouse in an empty larder.

In the margin of the ledger for December 1891, he wrote: *“A great deal of water today. Nothing else to report.”*

I like that. It has the correct proportion.

We are entering an era of great reporting. The men from the ministry in Whitehall come twice a year now. They bring portable anemometers in mahogany boxes with leather straps; they bring barographs with seven-day drums that use violet ribbons like typewriters; they wear brown tweed suits that smell of tobacco and metropolitan omnibuses, and they ask me questions about the "mean dynamic level" and the "phase-lag of the semidiurnal component."

I show them the books. I give them tea in the cracked mugs that have the transfer-print of the Duke of Wellington on the side. I listen to them explain that within ten years, the entire coast will be wired with telegraphic sensors that will feed their signals directly into an electric tabulator at the Admiralty in London.

They say that Station 44 is redundant.

They say that a boy in an office in Westminster will be able to look at a strip of punched paper and know the height of the water at Penmaenmawr, at Holyhead, at the mouth of the Mersey, and here on this slate spit, without ever having to smell rotting kelp or scrape the salt-frost from a north-facing window with an old table-knife.

They are probably right.

Machines are very good at knowing where the water is; they are only deficient in knowing what the water is doing to the people who have to live beside it.

When they leave, carrying their mahogany boxes across the shingle to the tractor, I go back up the iron spiral stair to the instrument room. I take the clean linen rag from the drawer and wipe the dust from the glass dome that covers the Thompson Gauge.

The escapement ticks: *click-rest, click-rest*.

The bronze cable moves. A quarter of an inch. An eighth of an inch. The stylus records that the moon has reached its perigee, that the sun is crossing the celestial equator, that the earth is wobbling slightly on its iron axis like a top that has been spinning since breakfast and is beginning to think about falling over.

There are three pages left in the green buckram ledger. When they are filled, I shall not ask the Hydrographic Office for another. I have four reams of plain cartridge paper in the cedar chest under my bunk, and twelve bottles of black iron-gall ink that I bought from the stationer in Carnarvon before the war.

I will draw my own lines. I will rule them twenty-four hours across and twenty feet down, using the bone ruler that my father carved from the jaw of a sperm whale that came ashore on the sands of Dee in 1868.

And when the paper is gone, there is still the bare brass of the cylinder.

A sapphire point is very hard. It can cut through brass for forty years before the stone is worn down to the mount. Even if the ink is finished, even if the office in London forgets that there is a spit of slate here with an octagonal tower upon its knuckle, the stylus will go on cutting its groove into the metal—deeper and deeper with every tide, until the sinusoid is scored half a line into the bronze, and the machine has written its own biography into its own ribs.

Outside, the gulls are pivoting again. The wind is backing into the south.

The tractor has reached the road on the far side of the bay; its iron wheels have ceased their dull clatter across the stones, and its gray exhaust has been torn to rags by the salt air before it can reach the height of the telegraph poles.

The water is coming back. It always does. It enters the iron pipe with a long, hollow suck that sounds like a man taking a deep breath before he dives into cold water. The copper float lifts. The cable sighs across the pulley. The stylus moves upward an eighth of an inch, finds the line for three o'clock, and begins its work.

As the sea breathes through the rock, the cylinder turns and the stylus rises and falls, drawing an endless, looping sinusoid—a cardiogram of the ocean’s ribs.

I have tended this machine for fourteen years.

Before me, my uncle tended it for thirty-two. When his knees swelled to the size of turnips and he could no longer make the crossing over the shingle, he sat in his Windsor chair by the grate in the village, looking down at his slippers, and told me that the sea had no memory, which was why men had to keep one for it. He was wrong, of course. The sea is nothing *but* memory; it is only that its memory is recorded in a script we are generally too hurried or too terrified to read: in the redistribution of gravel, the migration of sandspits, the gradual tilting of drowned forests, and the salt that enters the pores of the stone and waits fifty winters to split it from the inside out.

My work consists of winding the twin springs every Saturday at midnight, replacing the blue ink in the sapphire reservoir with an eyedropper, changing the paper rolls on the first of each month, and keeping the ledger. The ledger is bound in green buckram, four inches thick, stamped in gold leaf that has faded to the color of wet straw: *STATION 44 – HYDROMETRY & LITTORAL DRIFT*.

Outside, the gulls sit along the parapet with their heads tucked into their breast feathers, all facing the wind like weathered vane-cocks. When the wind backs into the northeast, they turn together without a sound, a silent militia pivoting on greasy stone.

***

### II. On the Cartography of Phantoms

In 1875, the Hydrographic Office of the British Admiralty published a chart designated simply *No. 2060: North Atlantic Ocean*. It was, by all technical metrics, a masterwork of Victorian empiricism. The soundings were sparse in the mid-basin—lead lines lowered four miles through black water take half a day to heave back to the cathead—but the coasts were ruled with razor precision.

Yet scattered across that gray expanse were dozens of small, irregular shapes marked with the letters *E.D.* (*Existence Doubtful*) or *P.D.* (*Position Doubtful*). There was the Isle of Buss, reported by the survivors of Martin Frobisher’s third expedition in 1578; there was Verde Island, which had appeared on Spanish rutters since the conquest; there was the Saxemberg Island, sketched with lovely topography by a Dutch captain in 1670, complete with two distinct peaks and a column of white smoke rising from a wooded valley.

They did not exist. Or, rather, they existed only in that specific stratum of reality produced by fatigue, optical refraction, and the human brain’s frantic refusal to look at an empty horizon and accept its emptiness. A patch of low cumulus catching the sunset at forty miles can mimic a headland of red granite with such fidelity that the lookout will swear he sees sheep grazing upon the downland. An upwelling of cold water will flatten the chop into the appearance of a shoal; a dead whale, belly-up and bloated with gas, has been entered into the logs of three separate schooners as "a black reef, unapproachable by reason of surf."

We laugh at this now, equipped as we are with synthetic aperture radar and the cold, unblinking eyes of geostationary satellites that photograph the planet’s skin every twelve minutes down to the resolution of an abandoned garden rake. But we have merely traded maritime phantoms for digital ones.

Consider Sandy Island. It sat in the Coral Sea between New Caledonia and Australia, precisely at 19°13′S 159°56′E. It was mapped by the whaling ship *Velocity* in 1876; it was incorporated into British admiralty charts in 1908; it migrated into the databases of the world’s maritime agencies; it was digitized, verified by algorithmic cross-reference, and rendered into Google Earth as a long, dark finger of land six miles long, floating upon the blue pixels of the deep sea.

In November 2012, an Australian research vessel, the *Southern Surveyor*, sailed directly through the center of Sandy Island. The echo-sounders beneath the keel showed forty-six hundred feet of clear water. The island had lived for one hundred and thirty-six years not because anyone had seen it twice, but because no one had possessed the administrative nerve to erase it. It was an institutional ghost, preserved by the simple, terrible weight of documentation.

I keep a list of these vanished places pinned to the wainscoting above my washstand:

*   *Dougherty’s Island* (South Pacific; seen 1841, erased 1932)
*   *The Aurora Islands* (South Atlantic; three distinct peaks of black basalt, surveyed by the corvette *Atrevida* in 1794; gone by 1840)
*   *St. Matthew’s Shoal* (Atlantic equatorial; logged by the Portuguese in 1516; vanished after eighty years of navigational terror)
*   *Nimrod Islands* (sub-Antarctic; reported by Captain Wright in 1828; searched for by Shackleton; nothing found but gray petrels and floating drift-ice)

There is something immensely comforting in their erasure. It suggests that the surface of the earth still retains a small, recalcitrant capacity to disown us. We lay our grids down like iron fences, we name every knuckle of stone, we assign three words from a dictionary to every square yard of the Sahara Desert so that an ambulance can find a dying man who has fallen from a camel, but the planet still flexes its shoulders now and then and shrugs an entire archipelago into the abyss.

Once, during a gale in my third winter here, when the salt spray was hitting the northern glass so hard it sounded like handfuls of dried peas thrown against the pane, I saw an island four miles out. It was long, pale, and notched at its western end like the sight of a rifle. It stayed there from two in the afternoon until the dusk took it. I did not log it. To log it would have been to give it an entry into the great legal machinery of disappearance; it would have required my successors to watch for it, to doubt their eyes, to write letters to Taunton asking for a hydrographic cutter to verify its absence.

I let it stay where it was: an optical sediment, a trick of the spray and the failing light, an island made entirely of cold air and my own wish to see something out there besides water that did not care whether I lived or died.

***

### III. The Acoustics of the Grave Shift

Between the hours of two and five in the morning, the universe is governed by an entirely different set of physical laws.

The town across the bay does not truly sleep; it sinks. The electric streetlamps, which buzz during the early evening with a high, neurotic 60-cycle hum, seem to quiet their filament chatter. The few trawlers moored to the town quay pull against their spring lines with a slow, wet groan that travels across the low water like sound through an iron pipe.

In the tide-house, the silence is not an absence of sound, but an accumulation of tiny, mechanical frictions. The escapement wheel ticks: *click-rest, click-rest*. The bronze cable shifts a hair’s-breadth across its grooved pulley as the Atlantic swells two inches beneath the floorboards: *hiss*. The sapphire stylus makes a microscopic scratching noise as it drags its burden of blue ink across the heavy paper: *scritch*.

In the fourteenth century, before the democratization of the mechanical clock, Europeans practiced what historians now call the *biphasic sleep*. They would retire at dusk, sleep for four hours, and then wake naturally around midnight into a period called *the watch* or *the dorveille*.

For two hours, people did not fight their wakefulness. They did not roll over and check the glowing face of a telephone to see how many minutes of rest remained before their labor was demanded of them again. They rose. They stoked the embers of the hearth. They visited neighbors to borrow a cup of lard; they recited prayers that had no petition in them, only contemplation; they made love without haste, in the warmth of coarse wool blankets, while the frost grew its ferns across the inside of the unglazed windows.

It was during this interval that the brain operated in a state that has since been almost entirely eradicated from the western hemisphere: an unanxious, non-productive lucidity. It was the hour of poets, of thieves, and of women who knew the properties of dried vervain.

Out here, the dorveille is not an interval; it is a permanent climate.

When you sit alone in a room surrounded on seven sides by salt water (for the well brings the sea into the very belly of the building, and the spray covers the roof), the mind eventually sheds its domestic posture. It stops preparing for the next interaction. It stops rehearsing arguments that will never occur. It begins to resemble the room it occupies: austere, slightly damp, illuminated by a single unshaded sixty-watt bulb that hangs from a braided cord of brown silk, smelling of paraffin, salt, and brass polish.

I have spent many hours examining my fingers under this bulb. They are the fingers of a clerk, slightly flattened at the tips from forty years of turning heavy pages, the nails scored with the fine longitudinal ridges that doctors call *onychorrhexis*—the small, harmless corrugated tracks that age leaves behind, like the tracks of birds across mud before it turns to shale.

We are so frightened of these hours. We invent entire industries of sleep hygiene, of blue-light filters, of white-noise generators that simulate the sound of an Amazonian downpour for someone living in a studio apartment in Croydon who has never seen a tree larger than a municipal plane. We treat wakefulness at three in the morning as a pathology, an insurrection of the nerves, a failure of the will.

We cannot bear the thought of what is actually happening during those hours: which is that the world is carrying on perfectly well without our observation. The trees are exchanging nitrogen through their mycorrhizal networks in the woods behind the headland; the deep trenches are being swept by slow, abyssal currents that began their journey when the Romans were mining lead in the Mendips; the stars are burning through their hydrogen budgets with the cold, mathematical indifference of a banker closing an overdraft.

To be awake and idle at three in the morning is to be an unauthorized spectator at the rehearsal of our own absence.

***

### IV. The Silt Economy

The town of Dunwich, on the Suffolk coast, was once a great port. In the eleventh century, it had eight churches, three monasteries, a mint, and seventy-eight ships of the line. It had a harbor protected by a spit of shingle that had been laid down by the longshore drift over two thousand years.

In 1286, a northern storm cut the spit in half. In 1328, another gale swept through the breach, choked the mouth of the River Blyth with three hundred thousand tons of shingle in six hours, and turned the harbor into a stagnant lagoon. The town did not die immediately; it died parish by parish, street by street, butcher’s shop by butcher’s shop.

The cliffs at Dunwich are composed of what geologists call the Norwich Crag—a fragile, poorly consolidated layer of sand, silt, and ancient shells that has the structural integrity of brown sugar. When the sea hits the base of the crag, the cliff does not collapse with a dramatic crash; it simply slumps. It dissolves. The water turns the color of weak tea, and the next tide carries the sand south toward Orford Ness.

One by one, the churches went over the edge. St. Felix went first, around 1540. Then St. Leonard’s. Then St. John’s. In the winter of 1904, the last standing church, All Saints, had only its tower remaining on the edge of the drop. Visitors would travel from London on the Great Eastern Railway to see it: an ancient flint tower perched on the very brink of nothing, with the bones of the dead protruding from the exposed earth beneath it like roots.

An old postcard from that year shows a human femur sticking out of the cliff twelve feet below the turf line, pointing out across the sea like a bowsprit.

In 1919, the tower went down. A local fisherman reported that for three days after the collapse, when the water was flat calm after the November gales, you could hear the bells ringing beneath his keel as the swell rolled the flint boulders back and forth across the rubble of the nave.

This is the silt economy. Every coast is a transaction.

Here at Station 44, the transaction is currently in our favor, though it will not remain so. The spit is accreting. Every tide brings seventy tons of quartz gravel from the headland to the north and drops it along the eastern flank of our causeway. The spit is fattening, crawling slowly southward like an amoeba across the sea bed. In two hundred years, if the charts are correct, this octagonal tower will not be in the water at all; it will be marooned half a mile inland, surrounded by sea-buckthorn and sheep pastures, its iron well choked with dry sand, its bronze cable frozen in its grease.

The villagers think this is good news. They believe that land gained is a victory, that the earth is reclaiming what the sea had stolen.

They do not understand that the sea never loses. It merely lends. It is a creditor that works on a schedule so prolonged that the borrowers mistake the delay for an acquittal. Every grain of sand that gathers around my granite foundation has been torn from the living room of someone else’s house three miles up the coast. The spit is built of dead gardens, collapsed sheep-folds, and the gravel paths where young women in long skirts once walked out on Sunday afternoons to look at the water that would eventually swallow their parlors.

***

### V. The Philosophy of the Diaphone

A mile and a half out from my spit, anchored in forty fathoms of black water, is the *Gull Rock Light-Vessel*.

She is painted the color of dried ox-blood, with her name spelled out along her sides in letters six feet high: *G U L L*. She does not move; she has no engine, only two thirty-hundredweight mushroom anchors hooked into the mud beneath her, and a crew of four men who spend thirty days at a stretch staring at the salt on the galley skylight and listening to the radio from Cardiff.

Her main voice is not her lantern—lanterns are useless when the sea fog comes rolling off the Irish Sea like a wall of sheep’s wool—but her diaphone foghorn.

The diaphone is an instrument of terrifying beauty. It was invented in Canada by a man named John Northey, who had originally intended it to be an air pump for clearing mineshafts. It consists of a slotted piston that reciprocates inside a slotted cylinder, driven by compressed air at forty pounds per square inch. When the slots align, the air escapes in bursts of catastrophic violence: twenty thousand cubic feet of air per minute, expelled through a horn made of cast bronze twelve feet long.

Its note is an F-sharp two octaves below middle C.

It does not sound like a machine; it sounds like the planet itself groaning under the weight of its own rotation. When the *Gull* sounds her horn, the air inside my tide-house does not merely conduct the noise; it thickens with it. The water in the copper well trembles. The mercury in the barometer jumps a hundredth of an inch. If you are standing with your forehead against the granite wall, your teeth will vibrate in your jaw.

The note ends with what acousticians call the "grunt"—a sudden, sharp drop in frequency, down into the thirty-cycle range, caused by the deceleration of the piston as the air is cut off: *BWOOOOOO-OH*.

The purpose of that grunt is acoustic survival. High-frequency sounds are scattered by fog droplets; they lose themselves in the mist like sheep in a briar patch. But that low, guttural drop at the end of the blast can slip between the water particles. It hugs the surface of the sea, sliding through the cold, dense air immediately above the swell, traveling twenty miles through weather so thick that a captain cannot see his own jackstaff from the bridge wing.

Yet there is a thing known to seamen as the *acoustic shadow*.

It is one of the most terrifying phenomena in navigation. A vessel can be two miles from a diaphone horn, running through a white-out of sleet and fog, and hear nothing. Absolute silence. The lookouts strain their ears until their temples throb; the skipper checks his dead reckoning; the leadsman calls out thirty fathoms, twenty-five, twenty. Still nothing. The horn is blowing with all the force of three steam boilers behind it, but because of a thermal inversion—a layer of warm air sitting like a blanket over a layer of cold air—the sound waves are refracted upward. They curve over the ship like a vaulted ceiling, leaping clear over her masts, and plunge back down to hit the water four miles farther on.

The ship strikes the reef in total quiet, while a cottage four miles away has its tea-saucers rattling on the dresser.

I think of the acoustic shadow often when I read the letters my sister sends me from Leeds. She writes of her children, of the price of beef, of the new municipal bypass that has taken half her garden, of the small, dull indignities of an office that uses machines to calculate what three clerks used to do with ink and nibs. Her life seems to be lived entirely within the acoustic shadow of something monstrous. She can hear the teacups rattling, but she cannot hear the horn that is shaking them.

She writes: *“The town is very noisy now, Ronald. Even on Sundays, you can hear the lorries on the ring-road. Sometimes I think I would like to come out to your station for a month and just have the quiet.”*

I have never invited her. She thinks the quiet out here is an absence of noise. She does not know that the quiet out here is an iron bell that has been struck so hard, and so long ago, that the human ear can no longer hear the tone—it can only feel the displacement of the air against the skin.

***

### VI. The Sediment of the Margin

What does one find along the high-water mark after the equinoctial gales?

I have kept an inventory in the back of the ledger for thirty years, set down under the heading *FLOTSAM, JETSAM, & DERELICT*:

1.  *12th October 1898:* One crate of pickled herrings, marked *Stettin*, unbroken.
2.  *4th February 1902:* The figurehead of a schooner, representation of a woman with her hair bound in ribbons, painted blue; eyes missing, turned out by gulls or surf.
3.  *19th November 1911:* Three hundred and fourteen wooden spools for cotton thread, empty, unmarked.
4.  *2nd January 1916:* A life-belt from the steamship *Persia*, sunk off Crete three weeks prior. (How it came three thousand miles in twenty-two days against the prevailing drift is a matter I have referred to the Hydrographer; he has not replied.)
5.  *14th August 1923:* The skull of a pilot whale, half-cleaned by sea-lice, filled with fine gravel that smelled of engine grease.
6.  *27th March 1931:* A crate of green glass bottles containing water that was fresh, though stale; no label, no corks, sealed with red rosin.

And then there are the boots.

Every beach in the world that fronts the open sea is a graveyard for left boots. I do not know why they are almost invariably the left; my uncle had a theory that sailors, when abandoning a foundering vessel, always kicked off their right boot first in order to get a better purchase with their lead foot on the gunwale, but this is nonsense. The sea is simply asymmetrical. Its currents have a handedness, just as the molecules of sugar and tartaric acid have a handedness. The Coriolis effect turns the water to the right in the northern hemisphere; perhaps it turns the left boots to the land and carries the right ones to the Azores.

They are always of heavy cowhide, nailed with square iron brads that have rusted into little nodules of red oxide like rowan berries. The leather of the uppers does not rot quickly in salt water; it becomes slick, black, and supple as grease. It takes fifty years for the ocean to digest a good pair of sea-boots.

Sometimes, walking the shingle at sunrise, when the light is coming flat across the water from the direction of the Dutch sands, I will see one of them sitting upright among the bladderwrack, looking so purposeful, so attentively planted upon the gravel, that I have to stop and wait for the man who was wearing it to take his next step.

He never does. He is twenty miles out, down in the deep holes where the cod lie, his bones turned into ivory buttons by the hagfish and his blue wool frock worn away into silt by the dragging of the bottom-nets.

***

### VII. The Night of the Great Glass

The fourteenth of January, 1928, was the only time I have ever seen the Thompson Gauge run off the paper.

The morning had begun with a greasy yellow sky, the clouds low and flat, moving from the southeast with a greasy speed that left no wake behind them. The barometer at eight o'clock stood at 29.8 inches. By noon it had dropped to 29.1. By four in the afternoon, it was at 28.3—a fall so rapid that the pointer had moved like the minute hand of a kitchen clock.

When air pressure drops that quickly, the atmosphere stops being a weight that holds things down and becomes a vacuum that sucks them upward. The surface of the sea rose four feet before the wind even reached us; it was sucked up into the low-pressure core of the cyclone like water into a syringe.

The wind hit at five. It did not come as a gust; it came as a solid wall of air that smelled of rotten sponges and cold iron.

By eight, the causeway was four feet under. By ten, the waves were hitting the eastern face of the tide-house with such violence that the water was coming through the mortised seams of the granite blocks—not as a drip, but as a fine, vaporous fog that hung in the air like the spray from an atomizer. The single light bulb swung in a six-inch arc, its braided cord creaking against the brass hook in the ceiling.

I did not leave the room. There was nowhere to go; the spit was completely submerged, and the granite tower was an isolated pillar standing in five fathoms of foam.

At midnight, the float in the iron well came up to the stops. The bronze cable went slack for half a second as a monster swell lifted the tower’s skirt, then snapped tight with a twang like a bass fiddle. The sapphire stylus, which had never climbed higher than the eighteen-foot mark on the ruled sheet, reached the very top edge of the violet grid, slipped off the paper entirely, and began scratching its track directly into the polished brass of the cylinder.

I stood by the desk, holding the edge of the mahogany table with both hands to keep my footing as the floor thudded beneath my boots. Every time a wave took the northern bastion, the iron pipe in the floor acted like a piston in an engine: a column of green water and gray air was driven up through the well-head, spraying against the underside of the oak desk with a wet, flat *slap*.

It went on for nine hours.

The terrible thing about such storms is not their fury; it is their monotony. After the first three hours, the human capacity for terror is exhausted. The nervous system simply runs out of fuel. The noise—the roaring of the wind through the lantern ventilators, the crash of the water against the three-foot stone, the whine of the bronze cable, the dry ticking of the clockwork drum that carried on despite everything—became an architecture. It was no longer an event; it was the world.

I sat in my Windsor chair, wrapped in my oilskins, and ate two cold potatoes with salt from a chipped saucer.

Around three in the morning, during the absolute height of the gale, I felt something move beneath the floorboards that was not the shock of the water. It was a long, slow shudder that ran through the granite from the bedrock up: a lateral displacement that lasted no more than a second.

The spit had shifted.

Somewhere sixty feet below my chair, the slate strata had sheared along an ancient fault line—a seam of calcite that had held since the Devonian period, giving up its grip under the hydraulic pressure of ten thousand tons of water forced into its crevices at fifty miles an hour.

The tower leaned.

It leaned no more than a fraction of an inch—less than the thickness of a half-crown—but when you have watched a bronze plumb-bob hang over an iron floor for fourteen years, a fraction of an inch is as loud as a trumpet. The bob had moved out of the center of its brass ring; it sat there, shivering slightly, an eighth of an inch to the north-northeast.

The stylus, still scratching its blind mark into the bare brass of the cylinder, made a sudden, sharp dog-leg: a tiny, permanent scar across the metal that no emery cloth could ever take out.

And then, as suddenly as it had come, the core passed.

By six in the morning, the wind had veered into the northwest and dropped to a moderate gale. The sky through the eastern window turned from the color of wet lead to that strange, pale, watery lemon that belongs only to the mornings after shipwrecks.

I went out onto the gallery. The causeway had disappeared. Not washed away—covered. Three thousand tons of gray flint shingle had been piled across it by the tide, forming a new bank ten feet high, topped with yellow foam that the wind was blowing away in clotted lumps the size of sheep.

The town was still there across the bay, but it looked different. The church steeple had lost its lead flashing; the roof of the fish-house had been peeled back like the tin lid of a sardine tin; two schooners were high and dry in the salt marsh, lying on their sides with their topmasts tangled together like the legs of dead spiders.

I went back inside. I took my eyedropper, filled it with blue ink, and lowered the stylus back down onto the paper.

The sea was falling. The float was sinking through its pipe. The bronze cable was paying out through the reduction gears. The sapphire point found the coordinate line for seven in the morning, twelve feet above the low-water datum, and began once more to draw its smooth, perfect, indifferent curve across the grid.

***

### VIII. The Ledger of the End

My predecessor, my uncle, kept his ledgers with a steel crowquill nib that made a thin, querulous mark, like the scratches of a mouse in an empty larder.

In the margin of the ledger for December 1891, he wrote: *“A great deal of water today. Nothing else to report.”*

I like that. It has the correct proportion.

We are entering an era of great reporting. The men from the ministry in Whitehall come twice a year now. They bring portable anemometers in mahogany boxes with leather straps; they bring barographs with seven-day drums that use violet ribbons like typewriters; they wear brown tweed suits that smell of tobacco and metropolitan omnibuses, and they ask me questions about the "mean dynamic level" and the "phase-lag of the semidiurnal component."

I show them the books. I give them tea in the cracked mugs that have the transfer-print of the Duke of Wellington on the side. I listen to them explain that within ten years, the entire coast will be wired with telegraphic sensors that will feed their signals directly into an electric tabulator at the Admiralty in London.

They say that Station 44 is redundant.

They say that a boy in an office in Westminster will be able to look at a strip of punched paper and know the height of the water at Penmaenmawr, at Holyhead, at the mouth of the Mersey, and here on this slate spit, without ever having to smell rotting kelp or scrape the salt-frost from a north-facing window with an old table-knife.

They are probably right.

Machines are very good at knowing where the water is; they are only deficient in knowing what the water is doing to the people who have to live beside it.

When they leave, carrying their mahogany boxes across the shingle to the tractor, I go back up the iron spiral stair to the instrument room. I take the clean linen rag from the drawer and wipe the dust from the glass dome that covers the Thompson Gauge.

The escapement ticks: *click-rest, click-rest*.

The bronze cable moves. A quarter of an inch. An eighth of an inch. The stylus records that the moon has reached its perigee, that the sun is crossing the celestial equator, that the earth is wobbling slightly on its iron axis like a top that has been spinning since breakfast and is beginning to think about falling over.

There are three pages left in the green buckram ledger. When they are filled, I shall not ask the Hydrographic Office for another. I have four reams of plain cartridge paper in the cedar chest under my bunk, and twelve bottles of black iron-gall ink that I bought from the stationer in Carnarvon before the war.

I will draw my own lines. I will rule them twenty-four hours across and twenty feet down, using the bone ruler that my father carved from the jaw of a sperm whale that came ashore on the sands of Dee in 1868.

And when the paper is gone, there is still the bare brass of the cylinder.

A sapphire point is very hard. It can cut through brass for forty years before the stone is worn down to the mount. Even if the ink is finished, even if the office in London forgets that there is a spit of slate here with an octagonal tower upon its knuckle, the stylus will go on cutting its groove into the metal—deeper and deeper with every tide, until the sinusoid is scored half a line into the bronze, and the machine has written its own biography into its own ribs.

Outside, the gulls are pivoting again. The wind is backing into the south.

The tractor has reached the road on the far side of the bay; its iron wheels have ceased their dull clatter across the stones, and its gray exhaust has been torn to rags by the salt air before it can reach the height of the telegraph poles.

The water is coming back. It always does. It enters the iron pipe with a long, hollow suck that sounds like a man taking a deep breath before he dives into cold water. The copper float lifts. The cable sighs across the pulley. The stylus moves upward an eighth of an inch, finds the line for three o'clock, and begins its work.
